title: AI-assisted procedural animation in Godot: fixing awkward athletics run-ups and the Fosbury turn
author: EyeApprehensive3982
selftext:
I’ve been using AI-assisted coding on Pixel Athletics, my free pixel-art athletics career game in Godot. This update was a useful reminder that an animation can run without errors and still look wrong.



The jump and javelin approaches had artificial knee lift and short strides. The high jump also had an awkward turn and a landing that did not read correctly. The work focused on the procedural motion code: leg recovery, foot contact and arm swing for the approach, then shoulder/hip rotation, back arch and back-first landing for the Fosbury. Pole vault and the different throwing events needed their own phase sequences too.



The workflow combined AI-assisted GDScript edits, regression checks and gameplay captures from Godot. The captures made it possible to inspect the movement, ask for corrections and capture it again. Passing code checks was useful, but it did not establish that the sporting technique looked convincing. The animations are still stylized and still being refined.



The attached 48-second trailer uses actual game footage; AI-assisted editing was also used for the trailer. Windows is free on itch.io, with an experimental Android APK beta that has not been tested on a physical phone: https://caseros.itch.io/pixelathletics



For anyone working on procedural characters, how do you evaluate whether a movement reads correctly beyond checking the code? I’d welcome feedback on the run-ups and high-jump turn shown here. This is my own game.
